clue.text: Band of players or cavalrymen, say?

indicators.note: say tells us the word for the cavalrymen is to be heard as spoken, not seen as spelt

parts.note: a troop is a unit of cavalry soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a band means musicians or a squadron of horsemen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks a sound-alike: TROOP, a cavalry unit, is pronounced like TROUPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a company of actors or performers touring together.

clue.text: Sounders for Mr Valiant-for- Truth on the other side

definitions.text: Sounders for Mr Valiant-for- Truth on the other side

parts.words: Sounders for Mr Valiant-for- Truth on the other side
parts.note: in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, when Mr Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river of death, brass instruments sound for him on the far bank

explanation.surface: A reader recalls the instruments that greeted a Bunyan pilgrim beyond the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The line quoted is Bunyan's: 'So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.'
explanation.definitionFit: Brass instruments that sound fanfares are what heralded the pilgrim's arrival in heaven.

clue.text: Arranged to get round a couple of reds perhaps

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters given may be in some other order, so they are rearranged
a couple of says the word for reds is taken two times over

parts.note: red, singular of reds, gives the colour word

explanation.surface: Someone arranges to get around a pair of red snooker balls, or a couple of communists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a couple of' takes the colour twice, and 'perhaps' is a soft signal that the doubled letters are then rearranged, following the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put in order has been arranged.

clue.text: Cut down Maltese Cross, insert gold one, that's the remedy

parts.note: to pare is to trim or cut down

indicators.note: insert tells us to place the gold and the one inside the cross

parts.note: Malta was awarded the George Cross, GC, in 1942
or is gold in heraldry
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Instructions for altering a Maltese cross by setting gold into it, which turns out to be a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maltese Cross' is not the eight-pointed emblem but the George Cross, awarded to the island of Malta in 1942 for its wartime courage; 'insert' puts gold and one inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Paregoric is an old opium-based medicine for coughs and diarrhoea, a remedy.

clue.text: Sweet order

definitions.meaning: a dessert or pudding, in British usage a sweet
the phrase '... order' means perfect neatness

explanation.definitionFit: A pastry pudding is a sweet, and tidy perfection is described as being in apple-pie order.

clue.text: Pirates to end in ruin — Kismet!

indicators.note: ruin as a verb tells us the letters of the words before it are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Pirates are fated to come to a bad end, as destiny decrees.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the four words 'Pirates to end in', fourteen letters; 'ruin' is the anagram signal, not part of a phrase 'in ruin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kismet is fate, and predestination is the doctrine that everything is fixed beforehand.

clue.text: Get many articles with this revolver

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, taken as many
a is the indefinite article
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A gun that collects plenty of items, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' supplies both English articles, A and THE. 'revolver' is not a gun but a machine that spins its work.
explanation.definitionFit: A turning machine rotates the workpiece against a cutting tool, so it revolves.

clue.text: Father leads Gallic giant in procession'

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
geant is the French word for a giant

explanation.surface: Dad walks at the head of a huge Frenchman in a parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads' places PA first; GEANT is French (Gallic) for giant.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant is a spectacular parade or show passing in sequence.

clue.text: Think highly of noble Italian family putting me up

parts.note: the Este were the ducal family of Ferrara

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word me is written bottom to top

explanation.surface: Someone admires an aristocratic Italian house for giving them lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting me up' looks like hospitality; 'up' reverses ME to EM in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: To esteem someone is to regard them with respect.

clue.text: Oppose the remainder, to produce see-saw effect

parts.note: to counter is to oppose
the balance is what is left over

explanation.surface: Resisting the rest so things go up and down like a playground plank.
explanation.definitionFit: To offset one weight with an equal one is what makes a see-saw rock.

clue.text: One turned out to be no big noise, vocally

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of the two words before it are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone proved not to be very important, when it came to their voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' reads as 'proved', but 'out' is the anagram signal working on ONE TURNED.
explanation.definitionFit: An undertone is a quiet, low voice, nothing like a loud noise.

clue.text: Though well-built, such a craft isn't dry, it seems

definitions.text: Though well-built, such a craft isn't dry, it seems

parts.words: Though well-built, such a craft isn't dry, it seems
parts.note: a well-made boat keeps the water out, yet the same word for it means drunk, which is the opposite of dry in the temperance sense

explanation.surface: A paradox about a sturdy boat that somehow isn't dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' also means teetotal, and the word for a watertight vessel is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel with no leaks is watertight, and slang for drunk is the same word.

clue.text: Beau ideal goes quietly to an old Spanish kingdom

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
Aragon was a medieval kingdom in north-east Spain

explanation.surface: A perfect gentleman slips softly away to medieval Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau ideal is the perfect model of something, a model of excellence.

clue.text: Raise the continental tax in the East

annotationWithheld.why: Raise the continental tax in the East (7) for ELEVATE: LE (the, continental) and VAT (tax) inside E...E needs two Es, but only 'East' gives one; no clue word supplies the other
annotationWithheld.clue: Raise the continental tax in the East

clue.text: Hybrid rose for the house

definitions.meaning: the heraldic rose combining the red of Lancaster and the white of York
a royal dynasty, as in the House of Windsor

explanation.definitionFit: The Tudor rose merges two emblems, and the dynasty from Henry VII to Elizabeth I was the royal house of that name.

clue.text: Reckon the deceased's property is about one thousand

indicators.note: is about means the estate goes around the next pieces

parts.note: a dead person's possessions are their estate
I is the Roman numeral one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone guesses that a dead person's estate is worth around a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to calculate roughly, to reckon.

clue.text: Russian type of mica

definitions.meaning: a person from Moscow, by extension a Russian
the common pale form of the silicate mineral

explanation.definitionFit: A native of Moscow is a Muscovite, and the commonest pale mica, once used as window glass in Russia, has the same name.

clue.text: Fed up with changing scene to moat, castle walls, etc.

indicators.note: in a down light, up means the word fed is written from the bottom
changing means the letters of scene are moved around

explanation.surface: Bored of altering the view, someone turns to moats and battlements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' looks like boredom; 'up' reverses FED to DEF, and 'changing' turns SCENE into ENCES.
explanation.definitionFit: A moat and walls are a castle's fortifications against attack.

clue.text: Humble Ohio origin of the twentieth president

definitions.text: Humble Ohio origin of the twentieth president

parts.words: Humble Ohio origin of the twentieth president
parts.note: James Garfield, twentieth US president, was born in 1831 in a rough timber hut in Ohio

explanation.surface: A note on the modest birthplace of a US president.
explanation.walkthrough: Garfield was the last president born in a dwelling of rough-hewn timber, a symbol of humble beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: A hut of unsawn timber is the classic humble frontier birthplace.

clue.text: Paladin in Arden

definitions.meaning: one of Charlemagne's knights, hero of Ariosto's epic
the hero who flees to the Forest of Arden in As You Like It

explanation.definitionFit: Ariosto's Furioso is about the knight of Charlemagne, and Shakespeare's lover in the forest bears the same name.

clue.text: Scholars in retreat pursued by sapper with this?

definitions.text: Scholars in retreat pursued by sapper with this?

indicators.note: pursued by means the first piece is followed by the next one
in retreat means the word for the scholars goes backwards

parts.note: BAs are Bachelors of Arts, graduates
RE, the Royal Engineers, are the British army's sappers

explanation.surface: Retreating students chased by an army engineer wielding a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' turns the graduates backwards and 'pursued by' sets the engineers after them. A sapper is a soldier of the British army's Royal Engineers, whose weapon this might be.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved cavalry sword is the weapon such a pursuer might wave.

clue.text: Mowgli's gray companion a monk ?

definitions.meaning: Grey ..., one of the wolf cubs raised alongside Mowgli in Kipling's Jungle Book
members of religious orders are addressed as ...

explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's wolf-cub is Grey Brother, and a friar or monk is called a brother.

clue.text: A second class highway, on the continent perhaps

parts.note: B is the second grade, after A
a road is a highway

explanation.surface: A minor route running somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the continent perhaps' is a definition by example: being on the continent is one way of being overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in mainland Europe is one way of being overseas, out of the country.

clue.text: Malignant Oriental, a Manchu, enters the dance

indicators.note: enters means the next pieces go inside the word for the dance

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
E is eastern, oriental
Fu is the first name of Sax Rohmer's villain Fu Manchu

explanation.surface: A sinister Chinese villain gatecrashes a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a Manchu' means Dr Fu Manchu, Sax Rohmer's fictional villain, giving his first name; 'enters' puts him, after the eastern letter, inside the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Something baleful is menacing and harmful, like a malignant look.

clue.text: Meat for the police ?

parts.note: stuffing made of minced meat has a name that begins with the word for a constabulary, so the police could be called meat of that kind

explanation.surface: A question about what police officers eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Forcemeat is seasoned stuffing, and the police are 'the force'.
explanation.definitionFit: A police body is called the force, as in forcemeat stuffing.

clue.text: Proverbial company of players

parts.note: the saying goes that two's company, and two golfers playing together make a pair

explanation.surface: A theatre company famous from a saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'company of players' suggests actors; the proverb is 'two's company, three's a crowd'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of people, as in a golf match for two, is the company the proverb allows.

clue.text: Man of property, three-quarters in gold

indicators.note: in means the three letters go inside the word for gold

parts.note: or is heraldic gold
three of the four compass quarters, west, north and east

explanation.surface: A rich man whose wealth is mostly in gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three-quarters' sounds like a fraction but means three compass points: W, N, E.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of property possesses things; he holds title to them.

clue.text: Kipling's age, when constructing tribal lays

definitions.text: Kipling's age, when constructing tribal lays

parts.words: Kipling's age, when constructing tribal lays
parts.note: Kipling's poem 'In the ___ Age' says there are nine and sixty ways of constructing tribal lays

explanation.surface: A literary allusion to a Kipling poem about primitive bards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constructing' looks like an anagram signal, but 'tribal lays' has too few letters; the clue quotes the poem's famous line.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Stone Age is the era of Kipling's poem about the primitive tribal bard.

clue.text: His tubbiness a form of cynical asceticism ?

definitions.text: His tubbiness a form of cynical asceticism

parts.words: His tubbiness a form of cynical asceticism
parts.note: the Greek Cynic philosopher famously lived in a large tub as a show of austerity

explanation.surface: Someone's portliness explained as a philosophy of self-denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tubbiness' means living in a tub, not fatness: the philosopher of Sinope made a storage jar his home.
explanation.definitionFit: The founder figure of the Cynics lived ascetically in a tub in Athens.

clue.text: Sleeves for a suit ? On the contrary

definitions.text: Sleeves for a suit ? On the contrary

parts.words: Sleeves for a suit ? On the contrary
parts.note: people wear their feelings on their sleeves; reversing the clue's idea, the card suit is worn on sleeves, not sleeves on a suit

explanation.surface: A tailor asks about sleeves for a suit, then reverses it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' means a card suit; the idiom is wearing your heart on your sleeve, so sleeves are for the suit, not the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: The red card suit is the one worn on the sleeve in the idiom about showing feelings.
